processing: Ginger, cinnamon leaf, nutmeg leaf, clove leaf, cloves and sappan wood are steeped in hot water with rock sugar. No fermenting or rolling is involved, and modern versions come as instant or bagged blends.
harvest_season: Not seasonal. It is a blend of dried spices and leaves sold throughout the year.
appearance_dry: A jumble of dried leaves, wood shavings, ginger and cloves, which is what gives the drink its name.
appearance_liquor: Bright, clear red from the sappan wood.
appearance_wet: Soft mixed leaves and wood chips, often left in the glass.
taste_profile: Sweet and peppery-hot with ginger, with a fragrant clove and leaf aroma.

brewing.notes: A rough guide for a whole-ingredient pack. Pour boiling water over the mix and wait for the red colour to develop. Serve hot or warm.

vintage_note: It has no vintages or harvest years. It is sold as a whole-ingredient mix or as instant and bagged versions, so simply look for a recent pack with intact aroma.
description:
Wedang uwuh comes from Imogiri in Yogyakarta, and its name is a joke worth knowing: wedang is a brewed drink in Javanese, and uwuh means rubbish. One look at the heap of leaves and wood in the glass explains it.

The recipe is ginger, cinnamon leaf, nutmeg leaf, clove leaf, cloves, sappan wood and rock sugar. Ginger supplies the heat and sappan wood the red colour, so a pale cup suggests too little wood or too short a steep.

It is drunk hot or warm, sweet and spicy with a strong fragrance. Give the sappan a few minutes to colour the water before you taste it.

The traditional pack keeps the ingredients whole. Instant and tea-bag versions are more convenient, but the whole mix is the more interesting thing to try. Around Yogyakarta it turns up in markets, restaurants, cafes, souvenir shops and as a welcome drink at some guesthouses.
history:
The drink is identified with Imogiri, Yogyakarta, but little is documented about when it first appeared. It was originally served with whole spices and leaves, and instant and bagged forms came later for convenience.

It has since been recognised as intangible cultural heritage in Indonesia.
